newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambians await results of disputed poll.
newsitem.headline: Zambians await results of disputed poll.

text.p: Zambians awaited results on Tuesday from presidential and parliamentary polls but the outcome, after an opposition boycott, was a forgone conclusion.

President Frederick Chiluba was looking forward to a second five-year term from Monday's election. Having barred his main rival Kenneth Kaunda from standing, he faced only four minor challengers who political analysts said stood no chance.

Former president Kaunda's United National Independence Party, refusing to recognise the election, was looking at different figures on Tuesday -- the size of voter turnout and the number of disgruntled voters' cards they had collected.
UNIP officials said they were convinced the boycott was a success and that masses of voters had stayed away.
To make sure, they had launched a campaign for people to hand in their voter cards and planned to tally how many they amassed in a rival anti-election count.
The Zambian Democratic Congress and others fighting the poll hope to mop up support of voters alienated by Chiluba's Movement for Multiparty Democracy but still keen to vote.
The MMD, formed as a broad opposition front to break 27 years of UNIP rule, won 125 out of 150 seats in 1991, leaving Kaunda's shattered monolith a humiliating 25.
Only about a quarter of the 4.6 million eligible voters were given cards for Monday's poll due to a flawed system that, along with press intimidation, was another opposition cause for complaint.
Western donors who share some of UNIP's worries about Chiluba, protested by freezing vital aid to the debt-ridden copper-producing country in the heart of southern Africa.
If the boycott flops, leaving Chiluba firmly at the helm despite UNIP calls for peaceful civil disobedience, donors may have to confront realpolitik and reconsider, analysts said.
It could also spell political oblivion for Kaunda, who took Zambia to independence from Britain in 1964, turned it into a socialist-oriented one-party state and ruined its economy.
Bending to the winds of change with the end of the Cold War, the veteran of southern Africa's liberation struggles agreed to free elections. Chiluba won on a free-market, democracy ticket.

Kaunda retired but returned to politics last year, apparently scaring Chiluba, 53, whose party then introduced a constitutional clause barring presidential candidates whose parents were born abroad, like Kaunda's Malawian father.
